         Austrasia, Burgundy, and Neustria. To this we add sev-
         en other lands which, strictly speaking, are not Frankish,
      but together form what we call Frankland. These provinces are

      and Thuringia. Each region retains some of its own history, laws,
      culture and outlook.

      Austrasia

      C
         ulture: Frankish.
         Territories
         From Reims in the west to the Weser in the east, and
      from Dorestad in the north to the plateau of Langres in the
      south, Autrasia contains the former Roman provinces of Belgica
      Prima (Trier), Germania Prima (Mayence), Germania Secunda
      (Cologne), and the east of Belgica Secunda (Reims).
        The Frankish heartland of Austrasia is mostly covered with
      dense hilly forests, with most settlements along the Meuse, the
      Rhine, and the other rivers. This region features important
      bishoprics at Speyer, Worms, Verdun, Maastricht, Trier, Metz
      and Mayence. It includes the duchies of Ardennes, Brabant,
      Champagne, Flanders-Artois, and Lorraine, and ecclesiastical
      holdings of Cologne, Liege, and Mayence.

           The duchy of the Ardennes is ruled by Duke
        Thierry. His vast domain is divided into five coun-
        ties: Arlon, Bastogne, Bouillon, La Roche and
        Salm. Duke Thierry is the Count of Bastogne, and
        the four remaining counties are governed by Count
        Galeran of Arlon, Count Aymon of Bouillon,
        Count Hugo of La Roche and Count Widogast
        of Salm. The duke’s military power extends to the
        surrounding abbeys of Stavelot-Malmédy, Prüm,
        and Saint Hubert. Even though these rich eccle-
        siastical domains are politically independent —
        called immunities — they serve under the duke’s
        banner in times of war. The spiritual power over
        the Ardennes is wielded by the very influential
        prince-bishop of Liege.
        Travel
           Roman roads have been partially preserved
        from Cologne to Amblève and Bastogne, leading
        further south to Reims; from Tongres to Bastogne
        and Arlon, leading to Metz; from Bastogne west-
        ward to Dinant; and from Cologne to Dinant.
           Royal relays are established along these roads
        every 20 miles or so. These consist of a village or an
        isolated palace where messengers can obtain fresh
        horses. Within the forest, such relays are often the
        only inhabited places for miles around.
     The duchy’s western frontier is formed by a natural barrier,
  the Meuse. This great navigable river is a genuine aquatic high-
  way, with such commercial river ports as Dinant, Namur, Huy,
  Liege and Maastricht.
  Economy and Trade
     The duchy generates much income from road and bridge
  tolls. The main agricultural activities are sheep herding and
  farming. Hunting is a significant source of wealth, as it pro-
  vides many households with fresh meat and leather. All no-
  bles sacrifice their first kill of the season to St. Hubert, or
  otherwise offer gifts to the local saint, in order to attract his
  benevolence.
     The forest contains a number of iron, copper, lead, zinc
  and even gold mines, giving rise to metalworking industries
  in a few towns. Many stone quarries produce good building
  materials. Most commercial activities are limited to local
  markets, while long-distance trade in swords and mill stones
  is in the hands of Lombard merchants who have installed
  themselves at Bastogne.

     Within the duchy of Ardennes, the royal family owns
  the following residential manors, or palaces: Amberloup, Bas
  Bellain, Bihain, Bullange, Chassepierre, Cherain, Chevigny,
  Lierneux, Longchamps, Manderfeld, Mellier, Neundorf, Orges,

  villas to the abbeys of Stavelot-Malmédy, St. Hubert or Prüm,
  and many others as fiefs to worthy vassals.

      to Dinant, Liege, Cologne, Trier and Arlon. The town’s earthen

      er defensive towers. Each tower is the home of a ‘tower knight’
      (see The Duke’s Retinue below). The central market place is fre-
      quented by Lombard and Frisian merchants. Next to the main
      square stands the church dedicated to St. Peter.

  Royal Palaces

Within the duchy of Ardennes, the royal family owns
  the following residential manors, or palaces: Amberloup, Bas
  Bellain, Bihain, Bullange, Chassepierre, Cherain, Chevigny,
  Lierneux, Longchamps, Manderfeld, Mellier, Neundorf, Orges,
  Ortho, Paliseul, Thommen, Villance, Wattermal, Waimes.

  north of the duchy, like Aachen, Attigny, Chevremont, Herstal,
  Jupille, and Thionville. Later, Charlemagne gives some of these
  villas to the abbeys of Stavelot-Malmédy, St. Hubert or Prüm,
  and many others as fiefs to worthy vassals.

        Most buildings inside the city wall are made of stone or
      brick. The entire palace compound is girded by walls pierced by
      gateways at four points. The natural springs provide warm wa-
      ter to the surrounding town, which has the wooden dwellings
      of merchants, a market-place, and the houses of abbots, bishops,
      and other dignitaries. Nearby is a hunting park bounded by a
      palisade and a menagerie.
      Places of iNterest
      iNside tHe city
        Gates: Four gates give access to the palace city. Each is
      guarded by scarae, who are under the direct command of the
      palace count.
        Aula Regia: The opulent Royal Hall is mostly used for
      general assemblies (usually in May and Autumn), official cere-
      monies, and to receive important embassies that Charlemagne
      wishes to impress.
        Cathedral and Palatine Chapel: Dominating the hill is
      a magnificent cathedral complex, linked to the Aula Regia by
      a stone gallery. The upper gallery is used by officers, paladins
      and the royal family. Inside the central Palatine Chapel, under
      a vast golden dome, stands the king’s golden throne. Visitors
      may admire the marble floors, the mosaics and painted stones,
      the sculpted bronze doors, and many silver and bronze statues.
      The most precious royal relics, like Saint Martin’s cloak, are kept
      here. On either side of the cathedral are basilicas. The bishop has
      his residence in one of them, while the other serves as the private
      chapel for the royal family.
        Treasury Tower: A high stone tower connected to the
      great hall which holds the chancellery, where the capitularies are
      written and copied by royal clerks. The second floor is the meta-
      torium, where the standard weights and measures used through-
      out the empire are kept. The third floor is the secretorium hold-
      ing the royal archives. The upper levels give access to the king’s
      personal treasure.
        Tribunal Hall: The palace count delivers ordinary justice
      in the main room on the upper floor; the scarae are lodged on
      the ground floor.

      rative springs (on a successful CON roll the curative water re-
      stores 1 Hit Point each day!), and a large marble swimming pool.

      place is heavily guarded at all times by scarae, and inaccessible to
      anyone but the inhabitants. The outer bailey contains the lodg-
      ings for officers, paladins, trusted personal servants (often young
      nobles) and important guests.

     South of Christnach, the black silhouette of a man without

     Three birch trees can be found in the middle of a small

  who were tricked by the devil. The trees now cry out and shed
  tears whenever someone whose soul is in danger passes by.
  devil’s stoNe
     Rumor has it that locals come to this large horizontal rock
  with a slit on top in order to make blood sacrifices or pacts with
  the Devil.
  faerie caves
     Along the meandering Semois river, several natural rocky
  cavities are the entries to an underground faerie palace. Its in-
  habitants are very discreet and do not like to be observed while
  dancing under the full moon.
  faerie rock

     East of Cugnon manor is a high rocky terrace split in two
  halves. At its bottom is a cave which is the entrance to a faerie
  home. When humans climb the rock, it slowly starts revolving,
  going faster and faster until the climber falls off.
  faerie table
     Along the Semois, south of the Tilman manor, a large
  square rock formation lies hidden in the forest. Anyone who ob-
  serves the dancing faeries unseen gains a fertility blessing.
  faerie tower

     East of Cugnon manor stands a secluded tower where
  White Ladies are known to appear at times.
  HauNted Hill
     On stormy nights, this steep rocky hill near Berthomont
  is haunted by the ghost of a knight who was slain by Saxon
  plunderers long ago.
  NutoNs’ caves

     A natural cave near the manor of Wilz is a home to some
  inhospitable nutons. Other such caves are located in the woods
  halfway between Roumont and Longchamps and east of Givet.
  NutoNs’ Pit
     On top of the rocky hill called Bérisménil, some nutons
  live at the bottom of a well. They are said to guard an ancient
  treasure.

      created a healing well. However, unfaithful husbands or wives

Three birch trees can be found in the middle of a small
  clearing west of Corbion manor, which used to be young girls
  who were tricked by the devil. The trees now cry out and shed
  tears whenever someone whose soul is in danger passes by.

  with a slit on top in order to make blood sacrifices or pacts with

  faerie caves
     Along the meandering Semois river, several natural rocky
  cavities are the entries to an underground faerie palace. Its in-
  habitants are very discreet and do not like to be observed while
  dancing under the full moon.
  faerie rock

East of Cugnon manor is a high rocky terrace split in two
  halves. At its bottom is a cave which is the entrance to a faerie
  home. When humans climb the rock, it slowly starts revolving,
  going faster and faster until the climber falls off.
  faerie table
     Along the Semois, south of the Tilman manor, a large
  square rock formation lies hidden in the forest. Anyone who ob-
  serves the dancing faeries unseen gains a fertility blessing.
  faerie tower

East of Cugnon manor stands a secluded tower where
  White Ladies are known to appear at times.
  HauNted Hill
     On stormy nights, this steep rocky hill near Berthomont
  is haunted by the ghost of a knight who was slain by Saxon
  plunderers long ago.

A natural cave near the manor of Wilz is a home to some
  inhospitable nutons. Other such caves are located in the woods
  halfway between Roumont and Longchamps and east of Givet.

  live at the bottom of a well. They are said to guard an ancient
  treasure.

      tHe duke’s retiNue

        At Bastogne, the duke commands five Knights of the Gates:
      Egier, Garin, Grimold, Radehart and Yvorin. In the count’s ab-
      sence, old Sir Garin acts as the marshal of the town castle. The
      ten Tower Knights are Adalhart, Baldric, Bernier, Chrodemond,
      Egduin, Guidolf, Odo, Radehelm, Thurold and Widochar.
      Father Jerome, the elderly chaplain, is in charge of the duke’s trea-
      sury. Thierry’s retinue is completed by his squires Amalwin and
      Onfroy, the horse groom Fremund and wise Master Salonius, a
      healer from beyond the Alps.
        All in all, Duke Thierry’s army strength totals around 70
      knights.
      The House of Clermont
        The families of Thierry’s uncles Aymon, Bevis and Doon of
      Rethel, are considered a separate and independent House. These
      three Ardennes lords consider their Ardennes domains as allods.
        Aymon: The sixth of Doon of Mayence’s twelve sons is
      vengeful and proud, but unquestionably courageous. The Count
      of Bouillon, he lives in the citadel of Bouillon and is married
      to Adelaid, a modest, forgiving and merciful daughter of King
      Pepin and the false Queen Aliste, and therefore Charlemagne’s
      half-sister, until Adelaid’s death in 756. Their children are
      Renaud, Alard, and Richard. Aymon is now married to Beatrice
      of Clermont, with whom he has twins, a boy and girl: Guido the
      Wild and Bradamant.
        Bevis of Aigremont: Aymon’s younger brother has a dark
      streak of vengefulness and pride and is nicknamed “the Beardless.”
      He is the father of the twins Maugis and Vivien of Monbranc.
      Maugis is a generous and loyal knight, and a wily enchanter who
      was raised by faeries. His twin brother Vivien was abducted at
      birth and taken to Spain to be raised as a Moor. He fought against
      his own father, but was captured and converted by Maugis in 766.
rightColumn:
Doon of Rethel: The eleventh of Doon of Mayence’s sons
  is an energetic, generous and indulgent count, who, strangely
  enough, has six fingers on each hand.
  The House of La Roche
     Doon of La Roche: The glorious and venerable Count of
  Cologne, Princess Olive’s husband. His eyes still sparkle with the
  fierceness of his youth. He delights in telling stories of old in
  which his wife and he play the starring roles.
     Hugo of La Roche: Duke Thierry’s eldest half-brother is
  the illegitimate child of Doon of La Roche and Thierry’s moth-
  er, Alpaida, and is a grumpy and bitter man.
     Galeran of Arlon: The red-haired Count of Arlon is
  Hugo’s younger brother, of whom he is quite the opposite; al-
  ways warm and welcoming.
  Eligible ladies

     The best endowed unmarried ladies of the duchy are court-
  ed by many suitors, who are either interested in their beauty or,
  more frequently, their holdings.
     Lady Ermeline: The young heiress of three demesne man-
  ors near Amblève is a very troublesome child and therefore kept
  under the strict surveillance of her uncle, Sir Egier of the North
  Gate. (Born 752, APP 13, Chaste 4, Reckless 17)
     Lady Giselinde: This extremely beautiful and haugh-
  ty young woman is reputed to be inaccessible to men. Her
  younger brother, Sir Odo, is actively trying to find her a
  suitable husband. The young lady’s dowry consists of Lavaux
  Castle and two allodial manors. (Born 746, APP 18, Chaste
  19, Proud 17)
     Lady Machteld: Kind and gentle, though not gifted with
  great looks. She holds two enfeoffed manors near Bastogne as
  her dowry. (Born 749, APP 7, Chaste 13, Forgiving 16)
     Lady Rolinga: The rich and mature widow of late Sir
  Norgast of Arlon has a very pious nature, and a pronounced
  taste for luxury. She holds no less than five demesne manors
  near Arlon. (Born 735, APP 11, Chaste 14, Indulgent 17, Love
  [God] 16)
  Important clergy
     Assuerus: The mystic Abbot of Prüm (–804).
     Beornrad: The austere Briton Abbot of Echternach (–797).
     Fulcaire: The erudite Bishop of Liege (–769). He is
  succeeded by Agilfrid (769–787), Gerbald (787–809) and
  Walcaud (809–814), all of whom are placed in this episcopal see
  by Charlemagne himself.
     Gerbert: The pious Abbot of St. Hubert (–809).
     Remaclus II: The powerful lay Abbot of Stavelot-Malmédy
  (–813). His battle shield is “or per fess Saint Remaclus et un loup
  de gules.” (a yellow field, with St. Remaclus in the top half, and a
  red wolf in the lower).

      The House of Clermont
        The families of Thierry’s uncles Aymon, Bevis and Doon of
      Rethel, are considered a separate and independent House. These
      three Ardennes lords consider their Ardennes domains as allods.
        Aymon: The sixth of Doon of Mayence’s twelve sons is
      vengeful and proud, but unquestionably courageous. The Count
      of Bouillon, he lives in the citadel of Bouillon and is married
      to Adelaid, a modest, forgiving and merciful daughter of King
      Pepin and the false Queen Aliste, and therefore Charlemagne’s
      half-sister, until Adelaid’s death in 756. Their children are
      Renaud, Alard, and Richard. Aymon is now married to Beatrice
      of Clermont, with whom he has twins, a boy and girl: Guido the
      Wild and Bradamant.
        Bevis of Aigremont: Aymon’s younger brother has a dark
      streak of vengefulness and pride and is nicknamed “the Beardless.”
      He is the father of the twins Maugis and Vivien of Monbranc.
      Maugis is a generous and loyal knight, and a wily enchanter who
      was raised by faeries. His twin brother Vivien was abducted at
      birth and taken to Spain to be raised as a Moor. He fought against
      his own father, but was captured and converted by Maugis in 766.

Doon of Rethel: The eleventh of Doon of Mayence’s sons
  is an energetic, generous and indulgent count, who, strangely
  enough, has six fingers on each hand.
  The House of La Roche
     Doon of La Roche: The glorious and venerable Count of
  Cologne, Princess Olive’s husband. His eyes still sparkle with the
  fierceness of his youth. He delights in telling stories of old in
  which his wife and he play the starring roles.
     Hugo of La Roche: Duke Thierry’s eldest half-brother is
  the illegitimate child of Doon of La Roche and Thierry’s moth-
  er, Alpaida, and is a grumpy and bitter man.
     Galeran of Arlon: The red-haired Count of Arlon is
  Hugo’s younger brother, of whom he is quite the opposite; al-
  ways warm and welcoming.
  Eligible ladies

The best endowed unmarried ladies of the duchy are court-
  ed by many suitors, who are either interested in their beauty or,
  more frequently, their holdings.
     Lady Ermeline: The young heiress of three demesne man-
  ors near Amblève is a very troublesome child and therefore kept
  under the strict surveillance of her uncle, Sir Egier of the North
  Gate. (Born 752, APP 13, Chaste 4, Reckless 17)
     Lady Giselinde: This extremely beautiful and haugh-
  ty young woman is reputed to be inaccessible to men. Her
  younger brother, Sir Odo, is actively trying to find her a
  suitable husband. The young lady’s dowry consists of Lavaux
  Castle and two allodial manors. (Born 746, APP 18, Chaste
  19, Proud 17)
     Lady Machteld: Kind and gentle, though not gifted with
  great looks. She holds two enfeoffed manors near Bastogne as
  her dowry. (Born 749, APP 7, Chaste 13, Forgiving 16)
     Lady Rolinga: The rich and mature widow of late Sir
  Norgast of Arlon has a very pious nature, and a pronounced
  taste for luxury. She holds no less than five demesne manors
  near Arlon. (Born 735, APP 11, Chaste 14, Indulgent 17, Love
  [God] 16)
  Important clergy
     Assuerus: The mystic Abbot of Prüm (–804).
     Beornrad: The austere Briton Abbot of Echternach (–797).
     Fulcaire: The erudite Bishop of Liege (–769). He is
  succeeded by Agilfrid (769–787), Gerbald (787–809) and
  Walcaud (809–814), all of whom are placed in this episcopal see
  by Charlemagne himself.
     Gerbert: The pious Abbot of St. Hubert (–809).
     Remaclus II: The powerful lay Abbot of Stavelot-Malmédy
  (–813). His battle shield is “or per fess Saint Remaclus et un loup
  de gules.” (a yellow field, with St. Remaclus in the top half, and a
  red wolf in the lower).

leftColumn:
Territory

        Burgundy is a large hilly, or even mountainous, fief from the
      regions to the east of the upper Loire and the Seine rivers to the
      valleys of the Saône and the Rhone down to where it meets the
      Isère. It consists of no less than thirty counties, of which the most
      important ones are Nevers, Dijon, Forez (Lyon), Montbeliard,
      Savoy (Geneva, Lausanne), and Dauphiné (Valence).
      Places of Interest

      autuN
        A prosperous cathedral town in the middle of renowned
      vineyards. Just outside the city stand the mysterious Roman ru-
      ins of a brick pyramid.
      auXerre

        Within the walls of the town there are a small cathedral and
      the royal Benedictine abbey of Saint Germain.
      besaNçoN
        A small mountain town with a motte-and-bailey castle and
      a cathedral.
      diJoN

        This walled city is the home of the dukes of Burgundy,
      who live in a medium stone castle next to the cathedral and the
      Roman baths. Anseïs the Proud’s father is the castle’s viscount.
      geNeva
        A walled town on the shore of Lake Geneva, with a cathe-
      dral and a royal mint. The local count is Oliver’s father, Renier.
      laNgres

        An episcopal town with city walls, stone gate towers, and
      a cathedral.
      lausaNNe
        A small town on the northern shore of Lake Geneva.
      le Puy-eN-velay

        A important fortified cathedral town. Together with Saint
      Giles in Provence, the magnificent cathedral dedicated to Saint
      Mary is one of the most popular pilgrimage sites in Frankland.
      Charlemagne himself travels there in 772 and again in 800. It
      contains a miraculous Fever Stone on which pilgrims lie down
      in order to receive its healing power, notably for paralysis and
      strong fevers.
      luXeuil
        A Benedictine abbey founded by Saint Columbanus on
      the site of a healing spring. It was completely destroyed by the
      Moors in 732, but later rebuilt. Nowadays many of its monks are
      Irish. Pilgrims come here to benefit from the curative baths. The
      current Abbot is Boso (768–780); later succeeded by Griomald
      (780–785); Docto (786–799); and Siliernus (800–821).

      Territories

      The ancient homeland of the Franks is a wide and fertile
  territory of river plains stretching north of the Loire and west
  of the Meuse, with the Seine basin in its center. Troglodyte vil-
  lages — where entire buildings are cut into the hillside — are
  characteristic of the Loire valley, while the lower Seine area is
  covered with groves and marshes. The Breton March in the
  west is hillier and less inhabited, while the regions around Paris
  constitute the more populated and rich agricultural heartlands
  of the Frankish realm.

     Also called the duchy of Swabia, the Alemannian territory
  lies west of Bavaria, centered around Lake Constance. It extends
  from the northern Alps along the west bank of the Lech River up
  to the region around Augsburg. The northern boundary roughly
  leads from Augsburg in the east along the Black Forest in the
  west down to Basel. The duchy is divided into 21 small gau; the
  local name for a county, as in Thurgau or Rheingau.

  many navigable rivers and lakes, of which the Rhine and Lake

Territories

     The immense archduchy, and later sub-kingdom, of
  Aquitaine roughly stretches from the Atlantic coast between
  Bordeaux and Nantes to the Loire River in the east and Garonne
  River in the south. It is divided into four important sub-duchies:
  Auvergne, Guyenne, Limousin and Poitou, each of which are
  themselves divided into counties.
     Though potentially one of the richest areas of the realm,
  the Aquitainian countryside has been ravaged by a decade of
  warfare and plundering. The land is completely ravaged after the
  conquest of Aquitaine in 769, unlike Gascony, which submitted
  peacefully. Pepin the Short destroyed most city walls and laid
  waste to enormous swathes of land. The population has suffered
  immensely, and this once-prosperous region with its rich Roman
  towns is now only sparsely populated, as many inhabitants have
  fled or been killed.
     The lands south of the Loire River have remained a
  world apart from the Frankish heartlands. The proud and in-
  dependent-minded Gascons were never really subdued by the
  conquests of Charles Martel and Pepin the Short. Therefore
  Franks are very suspicious of these “Romans.” Even during
  Charlemagne’s reign, Aquitaine remains apart until Louis is
  made their sub-king, even though most counts are Franks, rath-
  er than Gascons.
     Most of Aquitaine is rolling foothills and river plains. These
  once-fertile hills and valleys used to be covered with vineyards,
  but have been laid waste by the long and bitter war pitting the
  Bordelais against the Lorrainers and the Frankish mayors and
  kings. The country presents no major travel difficulties, and the
  climate is less rough than in the north, with warm summers and
  mild winters.

  hills of Auvergne are a taciturn, hospitable, headstrong and
  hard-working people. They receive a +1d3 bonus to Energetic,

The immense archduchy, and later sub-kingdom, of
  Aquitaine roughly stretches from the Atlantic coast between
  Bordeaux and Nantes to the Loire River in the east and Garonne
  River in the south. It is divided into four important sub-duchies:
  Auvergne, Guyenne, Limousin and Poitou, each of which are
  themselves divided into counties.
     Though potentially one of the richest areas of the realm,
  the Aquitainian countryside has been ravaged by a decade of
  warfare and plundering. The land is completely ravaged after the
  conquest of Aquitaine in 769, unlike Gascony, which submitted
  peacefully. Pepin the Short destroyed most city walls and laid
  waste to enormous swathes of land. The population has suffered
  immensely, and this once-prosperous region with its rich Roman
  towns is now only sparsely populated, as many inhabitants have
  fled or been killed.
     The lands south of the Loire River have remained a
  world apart from the Frankish heartlands. The proud and in-
  dependent-minded Gascons were never really subdued by the
  conquests of Charles Martel and Pepin the Short. Therefore
  Franks are very suspicious of these “Romans.” Even during
  Charlemagne’s reign, Aquitaine remains apart until Louis is
  made their sub-king, even though most counts are Franks, rath-
  er than Gascons.
     Most of Aquitaine is rolling foothills and river plains. These
  once-fertile hills and valleys used to be covered with vineyards,
  but have been laid waste by the long and bitter war pitting the
  Bordelais against the Lorrainers and the Frankish mayors and
  kings. The country presents no major travel difficulties, and the
  climate is less rough than in the north, with warm summers and
  mild winters.

Provence

      C
         ulture: Visigothic.
         Rulers: In the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign, most
         individual cities are held by a different Moorish wali, like
      Otrant of Nîmes and Tiebaut of Orange. From 768 to 771 this
      area is nominally under the rule of King Carloman. Once the
      reconquest of Provence starts, Charlemagne appoints new mil-
      itary leaders for the region: Duke Marcellin (780–800); Duke
      Lupus III of Gascony (800–814).
        Regional Modifiers: The thoroughly Romanized people
      of the southern coastal marshes, mostly Visigoths, are highly fa-
      miliar with sea trade and foreign cultures. They are open-mind-
      ed, but volatile and inconstant. Provence knights are at +1d3 to
      Selfish, Arbitrary, Trusting, and Love [family].
      Territory
        The relatively urbanized coastal region, between the Alps
      in the east and the Rhône in the west, consists of fertile fluvial
      plains, steep rocky canyons and valleys, and saltwater marshes
      around the Camargue delta. Strong winds often sweep across the
      plains, where mild winters and hot dry summers favor the culti-
      vation of olive and nut trees.
      Places of Interest

      aiX-eN-ProveNce

        The Moors are currently rebuilding this ancient Roman
      town just north of the Camargue.
      arles
        A Roman harbor town along the Rhone, with a stone castle
      and city walls, many large water mills and an aqueduct.
      avigNoN

        A walled Roman town at the confluence of the Rhone and
      the Durance, with a stone bridge and a cathedral which the
      Moors have turned into a place of pagan worship. Sir Anthony
      used to be the Count of Avignon.
      caMargue
        A vast marshy plain with many lagoons between the
      Mediterranean Sea and the Rhone delta.

        The largest trading port between the Alps and the Pyrenees

      house and is defended by the Castle of Lanson. Count John the
      Visigoth is suspected of secretly allying with the Moors.

      Moorish domination, Guymer is the Bishop of Nîmes.

Territory

     Thuringia is the small southern part of Saxony that King
  Pepin conquered, and as such it has become a frontier march sit-
  uated between the rivers Main, Werra, Unstut and Saale. The
  landscape is a monotonous hilly or mountainous forest, with
  many rivers and streams running through it.
     The Franks are still colonizing and converting the region,
  and the Duke of Thuringia is honor-bound to protect Austrasia
  from Saxon and Slav attacks. Once the Franks conquer more
  Saxon territory, Charlemagne creates the duchy of Saxony,
  which incorporates Thuringia, in 782.

Thuringia is the small southern part of Saxony that King
  Pepin conquered, and as such it has become a frontier march sit-
  uated between the rivers Main, Werra, Unstut and Saale. The
  landscape is a monotonous hilly or mountainous forest, with
  many rivers and streams running through it.
     The Franks are still colonizing and converting the region,
  and the Duke of Thuringia is honor-bound to protect Austrasia
  from Saxon and Slav attacks. Once the Franks conquer more
  Saxon territory, Charlemagne creates the duchy of Saxony,
  which incorporates Thuringia, in 782.
